analysis.title: Range-Bound Middle East War
key_insights: Base case: another US/Israel vs Iran escalation is likely from next week, after the 3 November US midterms, and is largely priced in. TS Lombard expects the oil price rise to be mostly discounted, with the next big move down toward $80/bbl.

Oil is back near $120/bbl, the level last seen in the war's early stages. Higher-rate expectations are aggravating fragilities such as French government bonds and raising fears about the sustainability of the AI investment boom.

The conflict has been in a mutual siege with periodic flare-ups since last summer. The US Navy blockades Iran's maritime trade from the Gulf of Oman, and satellite images show the tanker terminals on Kharg Island idle.

A 'dark shuttle trade' through the Strait of Hormuz (SoH), paid for by GCC exporters, keeps oil flowing. Double handling onto tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman lifts VLCC freight, with shipping rates to Asia more than 5x pre-war levels as of mid-October per the IEA. This widens the crack spread between crude and products, the main channel from the conflict zone to the world economy.
Houthi attacks on Saudi crude exports via the Red Sea reinforce the oil price effect. The conflict widened to Yemen after July.

Since mid-October Iran has sharply intensified attacks on shuttle shipping and threatened attacks on US bases across the region if Washington keeps urging ships to cross the mined route. Some commentators speculate Iran may carry this out before the post-midterm US strikes.

Red zone (1970s-style energy shortage and stagflation) is a tail risk. Three restraints are in place: munitions shortages (CSIS estimates Patriot stocks down by two thirds versus 2025), intolerance for US casualties, and economic blowback including an expected December Fed hike and a federal deficit at 100% of GDP in FY2026.

Green zone (pacified Middle East) is remote but is the more serious risk to the view. Routes are an Iranian concession under the blockade (the rial has lost two-thirds of its value vs USD in a year), a US-endorsed Iran-Oman agreement on SoH shipping lanes, or a separate Saudi/GCC deal with Iran.

Israel would likely try to derail any US concession. Netanyahu's better-than-expected election result leaves him acting prime minister with authority to order action against Iran during the coming weeks.
Concession progress could paradoxically raise red-zone risk if the Iranian regime concludes it is going under. Tehran has threatened undersea internet cables if the US escalates.
Saudi Arabia's position looks increasingly pivotal. Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani security officials met Iran's Mohsen Rezaei in Tehran on 26 October.
Even partial mutual concessions would likely leave oil in the amber zone, defined as $80-120/bbl, with oscillation between its bounds rather than a stable steady state.

tension_points.bull_case: Escalation after the midterms is already discounted in oil near $120/bbl, so the next big move is down toward $80/bbl as the market sells the news. Partial mutual concessions would keep oil in the $80-120 amber range.
tension_points.bear_case: Escalation could spin into the red zone of outright energy shortages and recessionary demand destruction, with US complacency after the midterms the most plausible path.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Iran retaliation that blocks all shipping or damages upstream oil capacity in the Gulf and western Arabian peninsula, taking oil out of the $80-120 amber range.

theme_stances.key_argument: Escalation is largely priced in, so the oil price rise will be largely discounted and the next big move is down.
theme_stances.evidence: buy on the rumour [of war], sell on the news
